title: Linus Torvalds Wonders If Linux's AI-Prompted Patch Flood Has Peaked
content:
Linus Torvalds Wonders If Linux's AI-Prompted Patch Flood Has Peaked (theregister.com) 6
			
		 	
				 The Register writes that "The worst of the patchpocalypse may be behind us, according to Linus Torvalds." In his weekly kernel update post, Torvalds said Linux 7.4 rc2 was a big release partly because it contained code he'd left out of rc1 because he'd been busy and it was already the largest such release in kernel history.
But Torvalds said the other reason rc2 was big was  "various AI fixes."
Such fixes are necessary because ever since Anthropic launched its Mythos bug-finding model in April, developers have been able to find more software flaws than was previously possible.  Microsoft, for example, addressed a record 974 flaws in September — its third record fixing spree this year after it whacked 622 flaws in July and 206 in June. Oracle addressed 1,449 flaws in a single month. That's many more patches than IT teams are set up to handle, yet they must find ways to deal with bugs more quickly because attackers are increasingly targeting flaws found by AI. 
Torvalds' post suggests that, perhaps, the worst of this is behind us. "This time around Alexei claims that on the bpf side at least the fixes are now coming in faster than the new reports, and that sounds lovely if true," he wrote. That's a reference to Alexei Starovoitov, co-creator and lead dev on the Extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), the project that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs within the Linux kernel.  "I think most other areas haven't reached that point yet, but it's at least a sign that we _may_ be starting to see the tide starting to turn," he added.  
The patchpocalypse has already affected Linux kernel developer  Lorenzo Stoakes, a principal software engineer at Arm,  The Register reported Friday:
Earlier this week he posted an email to the Linux kernel mailing list to say that he was planning to drop some of his workload.  He explained:  "Given the current throughput in the kernel resulting from AI-generated series, I unfortunately lack the bandwidth to generally be able to offer review except in those areas I maintain. [...] Apologies for doing this, but given the current trends I'd like to do something to make my inbox a little more manageable."
 
Stoakes told The Register, "I just want my inbox to be less horrendous. And yeah, AI is part of the reason; in general, it's gone from 'once a week' to 'daily' to 'half of what I see in review'."

report.summary: Linus Torvalds suggests the AI-driven flood of Linux kernel patches may finally be easing, with one subsystem now fixing bugs faster than AI finds them.
report.background: Since large language models became good at scanning code for bugs, open-source projects have faced a disclosure deluge. Anthropic's bug-hunting model, launched in April, let developers find flaws at a pace no maintainer team could match: Microsoft patched a record 974 flaws in September, and Oracle 1,449 in a single month. Linux's volunteer-driven review model — where patches arrive by email and are vetted by a handful of subsystem maintainers — was never designed for machine-generated volume. The result was what kernel developers dubbed the "patchpocalypse": inboxes full of plausible-looking but often low-quality AI submissions, mixed in with genuinely serious security fixes. Maintainers such as Arm's Lorenzo Stoakes began publicly stepping back from review duties, warning that AI-generated patch series had gone from a weekly trickle to roughly half of everything they saw.
key_points: Torvalds' weekly kernel update said Linux 7.4 rc2 was unusually large for two reasons: code held back from rc1 while he was busy, and what he called "various AI fixes" — patches addressing flaws surfaced by AI bug-finding tools.

The clearest sign of relief came from the eBPF subsystem, where lead developer Alexei Starovoitov reports fixes are now arriving faster than new AI-generated bug reports. Torvalds called that "lovely if true" and a hint the tide may be turning.

The underlying pressure is volume: AI models find far more flaws than IT and maintainer teams can triage, and attackers increasingly exploit AI-discovered bugs, forcing faster patching even as backlogs grow.

Human cost is real. Arm engineer Lorenzo Stoakes dropped review work outside his own maintained areas, saying AI-generated series pushed his inbox from a weekly trickle to daily to half of all review traffic.
Torvalds was careful not to declare victory, noting most other kernel areas have not yet reached the point where fixes outpace new reports, so the improvement may be local rather than systemic.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is an early real-world data point on how automated bug-finding reshapes software maintenance: the bottleneck moves from discovery to review, triage and trust. Expect tool vendors to pivot toward noise reduction, deduplication and patch-ranking rather than raw vulnerability counts. For developers, maintainer attention becomes the scarcest resource — well-scoped, tested, clearly explained patches will win out over volume, and AI-assisted submissions may face stricter provenance and quality gates. For regular users, the upside is faster fixes for serious flaws; the risk is reviewer burnout and rushed patches introducing regressions. The broader lesson is that AI scaling discovery without scaling human verification creates a new kind of technical debt across critical infrastructure.
report.tools: To follow or try this yourself: syzkaller and OSS-Fuzz for automated kernel and library fuzzing; the kernel test robot and the 0-day bot for automated build and regression reports; CodeQL and Semgrep for static analysis; b4 and lore.kernel.org for managing patch series workflows; and eBPF's CI tooling as a model for subsystems trying to outpace incoming bug reports.
